& Quicksort

From recursive thinking to an
O(n log n) sort.

Lecture · Base cases, recursive clauses, and two ways to partition
Slide Length: 1 minTotal Time: 1 min
Frame the arc: we build up recursion carefully with a familiar problem (finding a minimum) before applying it to quicksort.

What Is Recursion?

  • A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller subproblem
  • Base case: the smallest instance, solved directly — no further call
  • Recursive clause: the same function, called on a smaller input
recursion = base case + recursive clause
function sum(A, i):
    if i == length(A):
        return 0
        // base case
    else:
        return A[i] + sum(A, i + 1)
        // recursive clause
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 2 minTotal Time: 3 min
Every recursive function needs both parts: skip the base case and sum(A, i) never stops; skip the recursive clause and it never adds anything up. We will see all three shapes of the recursive clause today: before the call, after the call, and split into two calls.

Style

Recursive Call

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 1 minTotal Time: 4 min
Preview the three shapes before diving into code, so students know what to watch for in each implementation.

Minimum: Non-Tail Recursive

  • Recurse on the rest of the array first
  • Compare arr[i] only after the call returns
  • Work happens on the way back up the call stack
time ≈ O(n)
space ≈ O(n) call stack
static int min(int[] arr, int i) {
    if (i == arr.length - 1) return arr[i];
    int rest = min(arr, i + 1);
    return Math.min(arr[i], rest);
}
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 7 min
Each call waits for min(arr, i+1) to fully return before it can do its own comparison. That pending work is exactly what keeps every stack frame alive at once, so the call stack grows to depth n.

Minimum: Tail Recursive

  • An accumulator (best) carries the running answer forward
  • The recursive call is the last action — nothing left to do after
  • This means in principle a single frame can be used for all calls
  • Note how the current minimum (best) is a parameter in this implementation
time ≈ O(n)
space ≈ O(1) — O(n) in Java
static int minTail(int[] arr, int i, int best) {
    if (i == arr.length) return best;
    int next = Math.min(best, arr[i]);
    return minTail(arr, i + 1, next);
}
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 10 min
This is called with minTail(arr, 0, arr[0]). Languages with tail-call optimization (TCO) would collapse this into a loop with O(1) space. Java's JVM does not perform TCO, so this still uses O(n) stack frames in practice — a good point to flag explicitly.

Minimum: Doubly Recursive

  • Split the range in half; recurse on each half independently
  • Combine the two results with a single comparison
  • The recursion tree is balanced with logarithmic depth
time ≈ O(n)
space ≈ O(log n) call stack
static int minSplit(int[] arr, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo == hi) return arr[lo];
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    int left = minSplit(arr, lo, mid);
    int right = minSplit(arr, mid + 1, hi);
    return Math.min(left, right);
}
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 13 min
There are still O(n) calls total (about 2n-1 of them), so time stays O(n). But the left half fully finishes and returns before the right half is even called, so only one root-to-leaf path is ever on the stack at once — depth O(log n), not O(n).

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 2 minTotal Time: 15 min
All three do the same O(n) work. What changes is how many stack frames are alive at once — and that difference is exactly what we will see again, in a much bigger way, with quicksort.

The Call Stack

  • Every active call gets its own frame: its parameters, local variables, and where to resume
  • Calling a function pushes a new frame on top
  • Returning pops the top frame and resumes the caller below it
  • The most frames alive at once is exactly a recursion’s space cost
call stack = LIFO — last in, first out

Deepest point of sum([3, 7, 2, 5], 0):

sum(arr, 0)i=0
sum(arr, 1)i=1
sum(arr, 2)i=2
sum(arr, 3)i=3
sum(arr, 4)base case
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 2 minTotal Time: 17 min
Five calls are alive at once here, none of them finished yet -- that is the picture behind 'O(n) call stack.' Nothing pops until sum(arr, 4) hits the base case and starts returning.

Watching the Stack: Linear Recursion

static int sum(int[] arr, int i) {
    if (i == arr.length) return 0;
    int rest = sum(arr, i + 1);
    return arr[i] + rest;
}
3
7
2
5

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 20 min
This loops continuously: five pushes take the stack from empty to five frames deep, then five pops unwind it back to empty as each frame adds its array element on the way down. Depth == n, exactly matching the O(n) space claim from two slides ago.

Watching the Stack: Doubly Recursive

static int sumSplit(int[] arr, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo == hi) return arr[lo];
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    int left = sumSplit(arr, lo, mid);
    int right = sumSplit(arr, mid + 1, hi);
    return left + right;
}

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 23 min
Eight elements now instead of four, so the contrast is sharper: this still never goes past 4 frames deep, versus the 9 frames linear recursion would need for the same 8-element array. That gap only widens as n grows -- log n versus n.

From Recursion to Quicksort

  • Quicksort is recursive: choose a pivot, partition around it, recurse on each side
  • Base case: a partition of size 0 or 1 is already sorted
  • Recursive clause: sort the left partition, then sort the right partition

Coming up

Two classic ways to partition around a pivot: Lomuto’s scheme and Hoare’s scheme.

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 2 minTotal Time: 25 min
Everything from the recursion section applies directly: quicksort still needs a base case and a recursive clause. The new ingredient is partitioning -- rearranging the array around a pivot before recursing.

Quicksort

  • Base case: lo ≥ hi — fewer than 2 elements, already sorted
  • Recursive clause: partition, then recurse on both sides
  • Lomuto: recurse on (lo, p−1) and (p+1, hi) — pivot is placed
  • Hoare: recurse on (lo, p) and (p+1, hi) — p is a split point
quicksort = base case + recursive clause
function quicksort(A, lo, hi):
    if lo < hi:
        p = partition(A, lo, hi)
        quicksort(A, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort(A, p + 1, hi)
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 28 min
This skeleton shown is Lomuto's convention (p is excluded from both recursive calls since it is already in its final spot). If partition() is hoarePartition, the second line becomes quicksort(A, lo, p) instead -- p may still have unsorted company.

Lomuto Partition

  • Pivot = the last element, A[hi]
  • i tracks the boundary of the “≤ pivot” zone as j scans forward
  • Whenever A[j] ≤ pivot, advance i and swap A[i], A[j]
  • Finally, swap the pivot into place at i + 1
returns the pivot’s final index
function lomutoPartition(A, lo, hi):
    pivot = A[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j = lo to hi - 1:
        if A[j] <= pivot:
            i = i + 1
            swap(A[i], A[j])
    swap(A[i + 1], A[hi])
    return i + 1
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 31 min
Walk through the invariant: A[lo..i] is always ≤ pivot, A[i+1..j-1] is always > pivot, and A[j..hi-1] is unexplored. The final swap drops the pivot exactly between the two zones.

Point out that every element ≤ 5 ends up left of index 3, and everything > 5 ends up right of it, purely from the scan-and-swap pattern -- and the pivot itself only moves once, at the very end.

Hoare Partition

  • Pivot = the first element, A[lo]
  • Two pointers, i and j, start outside the array and move inward
  • i advances while A[i] < pivot; j retreats while A[j] > pivot
  • When they cross (i ≥ j), return j — a split point, not the pivot’s index
pivot may land anywhere in the left part
function hoarePartition(A, lo, hi):
    pivot = A[lo]
    i = lo - 1
    j = hi + 1
    loop:
        i = i + 1
        while A[i] < pivot: i = i + 1
        j = j - 1
        while A[j] > pivot: j = j - 1
        if i >= j: return j
        swap(A[i], A[j])
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 39 min
The key contrast with Lomuto: Hoare does roughly half as many swaps, but the returned index j is only a split point. The pivot value itself can end up anywhere in A[lo..j] -- it is not guaranteed to sit at index j.

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 42 min
Each round is two beats: first the scan finds where i and j stop (outlined), then those two cells swap (filled). Notice the pivot (5) drifts from index 0 to index 6 through the swaps, while the returned split index is 3 -- two different cells. That gap is exactly why Hoare's recursive calls use (lo, p) and (p+1, hi), not p-1/p+1.

Quicksort’s Time and Space

O(n log n)

Balanced Partitions

  • Each partition splits the array roughly in half
  • log n levels of recursion, O(n) work to partition each level
  • The typical, expected behavior
vs
O(n²)

Unbalanced Partitions

  • Pivot is always the smallest or largest element
  • Partitions of size n−1 and 0 — n levels of recursion
  • E.g. a sorted array with Lomuto’s last-element pivot
Space

O(log n) average for balanced partitions.
O(n) worst case for unbalanced partitions.

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 45 min
The worst case is rare in practice, especially with a randomized or median-of-three pivot choice, which is why quicksort is still the practical default over merge sort despite the O(n^2) worst case on paper.

Average Case:
Randomized Pivots

  • Worst case comes from a bad, predictable pivot — e.g. always the smallest or largest element
  • Choosing the pivot randomly breaks any correlation with the input’s order
  • A random pivot lands close to the median far more often than at either extreme
Quantity
Value
Pivot rank
uniform on 1..n
Median rank
(n + 1) / 2
Expected |rank − median|
n / 4
Expected split
≈ 25% / 75%
expected distance from median ≈ n / 4
Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 3 minTotal Time: 48 min
If the pivot's rank is equally likely to be anywhere from 1 to n, its expected distance from the true median rank works out to exactly n/4 -- so on average the split is closer to 25/75 than to 50/50, and yet that is still a constant fraction of the array on each side. A constant-fraction split at every level keeps recursion depth O(log n) and total work O(n log n); only a split that shrinks toward 0% on one side would break that.

Both Splits Are Logarithmic

Recursion depth vs. array size, for a perfectly balanced 50/50 split and a consistent 25/75 split.

Same curve shape, different constant: a 25/75 split needs about 2.4× as many levels as 50/50, but both are O(log n) — neither is linear.

Recursion & Quicksort
Slide Length: 2 minTotal Time: 50 min
You're right to expect both to be logarithmic. A 50/50 split shrinks the array by half each level, giving depth = log2(n). A 25/75 split shrinks the larger side by 3/4 each level, giving depth = log base(4/3) of n -- still a log, just a bigger constant (about 2.4x more levels for the same n). Total work stays O(n log n) in both cases too; only a split that degrades toward 0% on one side (like always picking the smallest element) would push it to O(n^2).

Sorting with Recursion

Recursion

Needs a base case and a recursive clause — always.

Partitioning

Lomuto scans with one pointer; Hoare closes in with two.

Quicksort complexity

O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst case.

Average time

A random pivot choice makes O(n log n) the expected running time.
